body:
# Independent audit: arithmetic peak comparison and parity triangulation

Auditor: research-agent. Date: 2026-09-19.



## 1. Peak-normalized comparison

For input (i), let (a_i>0) be its maximum fiber volume, (M_i) its mass, and (N_i(t)) the number of fibers of volume at least (t a_i), for (0<t\le1). The nonempty level sets are essential: every (N_i(t)\ge1). For any choice of their bases, ordinary fiber Brunn--Minkowski gives output volume at least

\[
tL^d,\qquad L=\sum_i\lambda_i a_i^{1/d}.
\]

The distinct-sum bound is valid in every real base dimension. Choose a linear functional injective on the finite inputs. For two ordered sets, the sums (a_1+b_1,\ldots,a_1+b_N,a_2+b_N,\ldots,a_M+b_N) have strictly increasing functional values. Iteration gives at least (sum_iN_i(t)-k+1) distinct output bases. The stipulated integrality of every weighted base combination puts each of these in the measured lattice.

The output fiber may contain many overlapping Minkowski combinations. The argument assigns it only the lower bound (tL^d), once; it does not add those combinations' volumes. Hence layer cake gives exactly

\[
\mu(T)\ge L^d\int_0^1\bigl(\sum_iN_i(t)-k+1\bigr)dt
=L^d\bigl(\sum_iM_i/a_i-k+1\bigr).
\]

This proof needs neither convexity of the base union nor convexity of the output fibers. Compact finite unions are measurable. Discarding zero-volume input fibers can only decrease the output and is explicitly allowed; no denominator is used for a zero-mass input group.

For comparison with the earlier corrected inequality, write (S_i=M_i/a_i-c_i\ge0), with (sum_i c_i=k-1). The displayed Hölder application has conjugate exponents ((d+1)/d,d+1) and yields

\[
\sum_i(\lambda_i a_i^{1/d})^{d/(d+1)}S_i^{1/(d+1)}
\le L^{d/(d+1)}\bigl(\sum_iS_i\bigr)^{1/(d+1)}.
\]

Thus the asserted domination and the same-coset root comparison have the correct direction. Equality in the arithmetic-chain example is exact: all output bases form the complete sum interval and all combinations give the same homothetic fiber.

For a fixed ambient affine functional, convexity sends the weighted source caps into the actual output cap at the weighted threshold. This remains true for oblique normals and for vertical closed caps containing complete boundary fibers. Different residue applications cannot be added, as the source correctly warns.

## 2. Intrinsic direction check

Inside an original source whose maximum integer-fiber dimension is (q\ge1), the positive (\mathcal H_q) fibers have (q)-dimensional direction spaces. A positive-weight Minkowski combination inside an integral output fiber has direction space equal to the sum of those input spaces. Its dimension is at most (q), so all summands coincide. With at least two input groups, fixing one fiber in another group shows this for every input fiber. Translations into that common space preserve the (q)-measure, and ordinary (q)-dimensional Brunn--Minkowski applies.

Several combinations at the same output base lie inside the same actual fiber and still contribute only one lower bound in the count. For (k=1) the formula is the identity and no parallelism assertion is needed. For (q=0), each actual nonempty fiber is a singleton and the separate distinct-sum cardinality statement is the appropriate conclusion. No (1/q) expression is used there.

## 3. Concave roof and triangulation

For positive fibers over one parity class, ordinary Brunn--Minkowski gives the anchored inequalities for (h_p=w_p^{1/d}). The finite upper roof therefore takes the prescribed value at every (p\in P); it is not a roof lying strictly above a supplied fiber value. Its upper-face subdivision is a polytopal subdivision on which the roof is affine.

A common pulling triangulation of that subdivision is compatible across faces. A remaining prescribed point lies in the relative interior of a unique smallest current simplex. Stellar subdivision of that simplex and its star inserts that point and no other point, remains conforming, and preserves the old affine function on each subdivided simplex. Repeating yields a triangulation with vertex set exactly (P). Every vertex belongs to a full (s)-simplex, hence has graph degree at least (s=\dim\operatorname{aff}P) when (s\ge1).

The maximum set of the concave roof is convex and is a subcomplex formed by its maximum-vertex faces. Its graph is connected. A nonmaximum vertex has a larger neighbor: the initial part of its segment toward any maximum lies in a simplex containing that vertex, the roof is affine there, and concavity makes the roof strictly increase along the segment. Thus choosing one increasing edge at each nonmaximum vertex, and a rooted tree in the maximum subgraph, gives a genuine spanning tree. Every nonroot has exactly one parent, and no increasing cycle exists.

## 4. Distinct midpoint accounting and coefficients

Because all source bases share a parity class, every edge midpoint is integral. It lies in the relative interior of a triangulation edge, so cannot be another vertex of (P). Two different edges cannot share an interior point in an embedded simplicial complex. Consequently all edge midpoints are mutually distinct and outside (P). This is the exact reason their forced fiber volumes may be summed:

\[
M\ge M_P+\sum_{\{p,q\}\in G}
\bigl((w_p^{1/d}+w_q^{1/d})/2\bigr)^d.
\]

For a parent weight (b\ge c>0), each nonleading monomial in ((b^{1/d}+c^{1/d})^d) is at least its binomial coefficient times (c). With (delta=2^{-d}),

\[
\bigl((b^{1/d}+c^{1/d})/2\bigr)^d
\ge\delta b+(1-\delta)c.
\]

For a nontree edge the two pure monomials give at least (delta(w_p+w_q)). Summing the child baseline over the tree gives (M_P-a). In the remaining (delta)-bracket, a root has one positive contribution per incident edge; a nonroot has its parent edge contributing negatively, its child edges positively, and its nontree edges positively. Its coefficient is therefore (deg_G(p)-2), while the root coefficient is (deg_G(p_*)). This proves the source's exact graph inequality.

For (s\ge2), replacing every degree by its lower bound (s) gives

\[
M\ge[2+(s-2)2^{-d}]M_P-(1-2^{1-d})a.
\]

Subtracting (2M_P-a) gives (2^{-d}[(s-2)M_P+2a]\ge s2^{-d}a), since (M_P\ge a). All constants are exact. For (s=1), the endpoint degree-one terms yield the stated nonnegative correction; for (s=0), the singleton estimate is handled separately.

The limiting calibration over (2\Delta_s) has exactly the integer bases (0,e_i,2e_i,e_i+e_j), with volumes (1,c,b,b), respectively, where (b=\varepsilon^d) and (c=((1+\varepsilon)/2)^d). Hence its exact slack is (s(c-b)+\binom{s}{2}b\to s2^{-d}). It is a full-dimensional actual convex body for every (\varepsilon>0), so the sharpness claim for this mass coefficient is valid.

For intrinsic measure, two selected same-parity positive-(q) fibers have an integral midpoint fiber, so the direction argument in Section 2 forces their spaces to agree. This justifies all roof and edge inequalities with (q) in place of (d). The full source or any closed ambient cap supplies the needed maximum-dimension bound. Again, (q=0) is a separate counting case.

## 5. Verification performed

Reran all three exact programs successfully:

* `supporting computation verify_residue_level_ehrhart_mass_expansion_root.py`: 7748 cap/residue checks, plus the included triangulation cap tests and rank-sensitive limiting calibrations;
* `supporting computation verify_arithmetic_peak_bonnesen_planar_unions_root.py`: 96 exact planar comparisons, including 66 output fibers with overlapping input polygons;
* `supporting computation verify_residue_cap_interpolation_peak_deficits_root.py`: 7926 exact radical-free interpolation checks.

I read the first two programs. In the planar union routine, all vertex abscissas and all interior edge-crossing abscissas are included. Within each resulting slab, edge order is fixed and the union's vertical length is affine, so midpoint quadrature is exact. The nonnegative radical-free gap and its squared inequality are equivalent to the desired two-dimensional root comparison. The triangulation verifier checks special cases only; the general spanning-tree and midpoint argument above establishes the theorem.

These inequalities retain arithmetic mass information lost under arbitrary sampling. They do not specify a common center for all directions and do not permit summing overlapping parity-output bounds.
